newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian firm to boost cotton crop, quality.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian firm to boost cotton crop, quality.

text.p: A Nigerian company has begun a project which will boost cotton harvests and decrease the contamination which makes most local production impossible to export, a company official said on Monday.
"When everything is up and running we should be processing 36,000 tonnes of good quality uncontaminated seed cotton," said the Afprint Nigeria Plc official.
"We have acquired the land, so we are already beginning work."
Industry estimates put last year's Nigerian harvest at a little over 250,000 tonnes of seed cotton, which translates into roughly 90,000 tonnes of cotton lint after ginning.
The Afprint project is based at Zaria in northern Nigeria, already a cotton growing area, and will start with a ginning plant and oil-seed mill in the first quarter of 1998.
The gin will process around 300 tonnes of seed cotton per day, while the seed mill will process 250 tonnes per day for local sales of edible oil.
"The project should take 18 to 24 months and cost around one billion naira," the official said.
An outgrower scheme covering an estimated 25,000 hectares will supply farmers with seeds and technical expertise.

Afprint subsidiary Afcott already has a 4,500 cotton estate and 5,000 hectare outgrower scheme in north-eastern Yola, one of the few places which produces cotton that is not contaminated by polyethene fibres and can be exported.
Nigerian cotton is affected by contamination from the bags which are used in transporting it instead of more expensive jute sacks.
The lower quality cotton is adequate for the Nigerian and West African domestic cloth market but unsuitable for export.

Millers which are also aiming at exports of thread and cloth, including Afprint, have in the past been forced to rely on imported cotton from neighbouring Benin, where contamination is much less of a problem, analysts say.
"As the farmers will be trained from the start we should be able to eliminate contamination and produce an exportable product," the official said.
Falling local demand due to economic recession has left many of Nigeria's textile mills running at as low as 20 percent of capacity utilisation.
Reports from northern Nigeria say a higher number of farmers are growing cotton in 1996. This is because a government fertiliser subsidy has had the effect of making it virtually unavailable.
Farmers in Zamfara state told the News Agency of Nigeria last week that as cotton needed only insecticide they had planted it instead of maize or sorghum.
However, industry sources say that patchy rainfall may lead to a harvest roughly the same as last year's. Output figures are expected around January.
